'''''Emilia fosbergii''''' is a species of plant in the [[Asteraceae|sunflower family]].<ref>[https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/12971251#page/42/mode/1up Nicolson, Dan Henry 1975.  Phytologia 32(1): 34]</ref><ref>[http://www.tropicos.org/Name/2702411 Tropicos, ''Emilia fosbergii'' Nicolson ]</ref><ref>Nicolson, D. H. 1980. A summary of cytological information on Emilia and the taxonomy of four Pacific taxa of ''Emilia'' (Asteraceae: Senecioneae). Systematic Botany 5: 391–407.</ref> It is commonly known in the United States as '''Florida tasselflower'''.<ref name="NRCS">{{cite web|author=Natural Resources Conservation Service (NRCS)|authorlink=Natural Resources Conservation Service|title=PLANTS Profile, ''Emilia fosbergii''|url=https://plants.usda.gov/java/profile?symbol=EMFO|access-date=2008-05-21|work=The PLANTS Database|publisher=[[United States Department of Agriculture]]}}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
''Emilia fosbergii'' has been collected in many places for many years, the specimens regarded as belonging to ''[[Emilia coccinea|E. coccinea]], [[Emilia sagittata|E. sagittata]], ''or'' [[Emilia javanica|E. javanica]].'' A reexamination of a large number of specimens led [[Dan Henry Nicolson|Nicolson]] to recognize it as a distinct species in 1975. He named the species in honor of [[Francis Raymond Fosberg]].<ref>[https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/12971251#page/41/mode/1up Nicolson, Dan Henry 1975.  Phytologia 32(1): 33-34]</ref>

==Distribution==
''Emilia fosbergii'' is widely distributed in tropical and semitropical parts of the world: [[Africa]], [[South Asia|South]] and [[Southeast Asia|Southeast]] [[Asia]], northern [[Australia]], [[North America|North]] and [[South America]], and various oceanic islands. Its region of origin is the subject of some dispute; some say it is native to [[Africa]], while others say [[Asia]] or [[South America]].<ref name="h">{{Cite web|title=Flann, C (ed) 2009+ Global Compositae Checklist|url=http://dixon.iplantcollaborative.org/CompositaeWeb/Default.aspx?Page=NameDetails&TabNum=3&nameId=3e4b4752-5915-4e59-8f15-07aad72d4b5e|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://archive.today/20141120231935/http://dixon.iplantcollaborative.org/CompositaeWeb/Default.aspx?Page=NameDetails&TabNum=3&nameId=3e4b4752-5915-4e59-8f15-07aad72d4b5e|archive-date=2014-11-20|access-date=2014-11-20}}</ref><ref>[http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=242426457 Flora of North America, Florida tasselflower, ''Emilia fosbergii'' Nicolson, Phytologia. 32: 34. 1975. ]</ref><ref>[http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=242426457 Flora of China Vol. 20-21 Page 543 <big>缨荣花</big> ying rong hua ''Emilia fosbergii'' Nicolson, Phytologia. 32: 34. 1975. ]</ref> It is reportedly naturalized in scattered locations in the United States, including [[Puerto Rico]], and the [[Virgin Islands]].<ref name="h" /><ref>[http://bonap.net/MapGallery/County/Emilia%20fosbergii.png Biota of North America Program 2013 county distribution map]</ref>

==Description==
''Emilia fosbergii'' is an [[Annual plant|annual]] herb, growing up to 100 cm (40 inches) tall. It generally has only one central stem, sometimes branching but other times not. Each [[flower head]] can contain more than 60 pink, purple, or red [[disc floret]]s, however, no [[ray florets]] are present.<ref>[http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=242426457 Flora of North America, Florida tasselflower, ''Emilia fosbergii'' Nicolson]</ref> It produces seeds with hairs intended for wind dispersal. <ref>[https://www.cabidigitallibrary.org/doi/full/10.1079/cabicompendium.114086] CABI Compendium, ''Emilia fosbergii'' (Florida tassel-flower), Rojas-Sandoval, Acevedo-Rodriguez.</ref>
